headline: China’s hollow-core fiber trial pushes 51.3 Tb/s over 128 miles without signal regeneration
summary: Chinese firm YOFC, China Telecom, and Dekoli achieved a world-record 51.3 Tb/s transmission over 206.5 km using hollow-core fiber. This was done without signal regeneration and only with conventional erbium-doped fiber amplifiers.
details: Chinese firm Yangtze Optical Fiber and Cable Joint Stock Limited Company (YOFC), in collaboration with China Telecom and optical equipment maker Dekoli, completed the world’s first field trial of hollow-core fiber (HCF) wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM). They achieved an unprecedented aggregate transmission capacity of 51.3 Tb/s over roughly 128 miles (206.5 km) without signal regeneration. This sets a new world record for unrepeatered WDM capacity-distance performance.

The record was achieved using only conventional erbium-doped fiber amplifier amplification, avoiding the remote-pumped boosters typically needed for such long unrepeatered spans. This combination of high capacity, long distance, and specific amplification approach in a live network marks a significant leap from previous lab-only results.

Hollow-core fiber is a next-generation optical data transmission medium that guides light through an air-filled channel, unlike conventional glass fiber. Light travels roughly 1.5 times faster through air, significantly cutting latency. The air core also sidesteps nonlinear distortion and dispersion inherent in silica.

In theory, HCF enables far more data over greater distances with fewer amplification points. Historically, commercial HCF had higher attenuation than silica fiber, limiting signal reach. This trial's 200 km-plus unrepeatered span demonstrates significant progress in overcoming this limitation.

The collaborators achieved this through two main innovations. At the system level, they used a self-developed optimization scheme for per-wavelength rate and channel power allocation. This allowed the system to adapt each channel to link conditions, reducing capacity losses from gas-absorption peaks.

On the hardware side, researchers built a high-power amplifier using a cascaded dual-gain-unit architecture and a multi-element doping design. This achieved a maximum output of 33.5 dBm while maintaining flat gain across the operating band, further extending the unrepeatered span without remote-pumped amplifiers.

headline_marked: Google warns [[EU rules could lead to search data hacks]] & Android fraud
headline: Google warns EU rules could lead to search data hacks & Android fraud
summary: Google's top security staff warns that proposed EU Digital Markets Act changes, aimed at opening up its search data and Android, could significantly increase fraud and cybercrime in Europe.
details: Google's top privacy and security staff warn that upcoming EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) changes could lead to people's search queries being hacked and a rise in cybercrime. These changes are designed to open up Google's search data and Android OS to competitors.

The European Commission is set to make final decisions next month on Google Search and Android interoperability under the DMA. This act, adopted in late 2022, aims to force dominant Big Tech firms to open their markets and foster competition.

Heather Adkins, Google's VP of security engineering, expressed concerns about both Search and Android proposals. She predicts a "significant increase in fraud" on Android within weeks if implemented as described.
Adkins also claims that proposed changes to Google Search could allow bad actors to de-anonymize search queries. Shared search data with smaller companies could become a target for criminal hackers.

The EU's proposals require Google to provide online search engines with "on par" access to search data, including user queries and metadata. This unique dataset has historically only been accessible to Google.
While the proposals include anonymization methods and contracts to prevent reidentification, Google's opposition has grown vocal as the July 27 deadline for final decisions approaches.

Some Google competitors and independent researchers, who could benefit from the data access, argue that the privacy and security impacts are less severe than Google suggests. They have pointed out potential ways the plans could work.

The DMA designates large market share tech companies as "gatekeepers," compelling them to open systems and data. Google's search business, holding an estimated 90% of the worldwide market, is a key focus.
